behaviour_notes: Component processes started by executionEngine.runComponent (workflows, execute_component, agent tools) no longer get the server's process.env. They now get buildComponentEnv(), which is the MCP allow-list from core/mcpChildEnv.js (PATH, HOME, TMP, locale, proxy, NODE_ENV, NPM_CONFIG_*, TERM) plus NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS is passed so components that fetch web pages keep working on self-hosts behind a TLS-inspecting proxy. NODE_OPTIONS and all secrets (MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY, DATABASE_URL, OPAQUE_SERVER_SETUP, provider keys, and any new name) are dropped. None of the shipped components in components/ read process.env, and per-user credentials still reach components on stdin (_accessToken, _appPassword and so on), so a user should notice no difference. The only exception is a custom, user-written component that read a server env var: it now sees undefined there. API shapes, status codes and UI are unchanged. executionEngine now also exports runComponent and buildComponentEnv, for the test. In agentChat.js and agentTools.js only comments changed, because the old wording said the component runs "with the server's env".
open_questions: Not done, as the scope says: (1) removing component_designer from the default org grant (stores/user/schema.js:266) and making /create-component admin-only are product decisions for the owner; (2) Part 2 is not started: running components in a throwaway container or a separate uid, without docker.sock and without /proc access to the server, with egress limited to public addresses. Until then, component code still runs as the server uid, can read /proc/<server-pid>/environ and can use the mounted docker.sock. So the env fix closes the direct leak, but not the whole hole. Also outside this scope: componentManager.installDependencies still runs `npm install` with the full server env, so install scripts of packages on ALLOWED_DEPENDENCIES see the secrets. The allowlist limits the risk, but the same allow-listed env (plus npm_config_* variables) could be passed there; I left it alone because it could break native installs (better-sqlite3 prebuild/node-gyp). Unrelated bug spotted in executionEngine.js (not changed): the trigger-watcher path calls the async watcherStateStore.getWatcherState and saveWatcherState without await, so prevState?.items is always undefined and every item counts as 'added'.

behaviour_notes:
The bootstrap and diagnose checks still read the X-Beeflow-NC-Base-Url header. That header comes from an unauthenticated request. verifyNcInstance (server/auth/connectorBootstrap.js) now fetches it with nextcloudFetch from integrations/nextcloudTarget.js instead of the global fetch. This is the same SSRF gate that the user Nextcloud URL and Talk bot calls already go through.

What changes:
- Loopback, private, link-local and cloud-metadata targets are refused before any request is sent. So are URLs that contain a username or password.
- Redirect hops are re-checked when each connection opens.
- A refusal is wrapped as "NC capabilities unreachable: <reason>". For bootstrap it therefore takes the existing branch: 403 with code nc_capabilities_unreachable and the existing remediation text. Diagnose returns its existing 403 "NC ownership verification failed". The response shape and status codes are unchanged.

What a user could notice: a self-hosted server whose Nextcloud is on a LAN or Docker-internal address now gets nc_capabilities_unreachable at bootstrap or diagnose. The error detail names the fix: set NEXTCLOUD_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS=1. Such setups already need that flag for the per-user Nextcloud URL and nextcloudClient. A public Nextcloud is unaffected. So is the dev sandbox, because docker-compose.dev.yml sets BEEFLOW_BOOTSTRAP_SKIP_VERIFY=true.

verifyNcInstance is now also exported in module.exports.helpers so it can be tested.
open_questions:
1. Not done because they would change behaviour:
   - Replacing e.message with fixed error codes in the 403 bodies (bootstrap `error`, diagnose `detail`).
   - Dropping the reported instance id from the mismatch message (`server=<id>`).
   - A zod rule that only accepts https in the base-URL header. This would break self-hosts that use plain http on a LAN.
   With private targets now refused, these messages only describe public hosts that anyone can query directly.

2. A gap in integrations/nextcloudTarget.js (outside my lane): with NEXTCLOUD_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS=1, nextcloudFetch uses the plain global fetch, which follows redirects without checking them again. A public Nextcloud URL could then redirect to 169.254.169.254. The metadata block only applies to the first URL. Suggested fix: when the flag is set, use redirect: 'manual' and re-run assertAllowedNextcloudHost on each hop, or use a dispatcher that blocks only metadata addresses.

3. NEXTCLOUD_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS is not mentioned in any .env.example or in docs/docs/connector/troubleshooting.md. LAN self-hosters who now hit nc_capabilities_unreachable would benefit from a line there.

behaviour_notes:
Users will notice one thing: when two people edit a site's pages at the same time (or one edits through a pod with a stale cache), a page created, renamed, reordered or deleted by one of them no longer silently disappears. Error messages ('Project not found', 'Page not found', 'Slug "x" is reserved'), return values and API shapes are unchanged.

Two small, rare differences:
- If two people create a page with the same slug at nearly the same moment, the second one now gets the next free slug ('about-2'), and that page's own record is rewritten to match.
- updatePageMeta now saves the site's page list before the page's own record (it used to be the other way round). If the second write fails, the list has the new slug or title and the page record keeps the old one, where before it was the reverse.

Under the hood:
- createPage, updatePageMeta, setHomepage, reorderPages, removePage and renameProject now read and write the site through the new mutateProject helper. It calls configStore.mutateConfig, which holds a lock that works across replicas and reads the database, not the 60s cache.
- createPage first reads the site fresh from the database to check it exists and plan the slug, then writes the page record, then picks the final slug again under the lock.
- getProject returns a structuredClone, and its lazy migration (now the function migrateSite) runs on that copy. So neither the migration nor an edit whose save fails ends up in the cache.
- getConfigFresh caches a structuredClone and returns its own private copy.
- setProject behaves as before; its sanitising and index-update code moved into the helpers sanitizeSite and touchProjectsIndexEntry.
open_questions:
- setProject (the editor's full-site save of header, footer, design and so on) still overwrites the whole site record, and the last save wins. That is deliberate, because the client sends the complete site. As a result, a full-site save from an editor whose page list is stale can still undo a page change made at the same moment on another pod. Closing that would need a version or ETag check, which changes API behaviour, so I left it out.
- The index update after each site write (touchProjectsIndexEntry) still uses the plain read-then-write path, as the existing comment allows: a lost update there only costs a stale timestamp or name.
- getConfig itself still returns the shared cached object; only getProject now clones it. Other callers of getConfig that change the result in place are outside this finding.

behaviour_notes: Before the fix, the Google Meet auto-import discovery and the ISO evidence collector both used advisory-lock key 0xBEEF10A. While one job held the lock, the other skipped its tick on every pod without logging anything. In ticks.js, the Meet discovery now takes a named lock through withNamedLock(pool, 'beeflow:job:gmeetAutoImportDiscovery', ...) from jobs/lib/namedLock.js. Everything else works as before. Discovery still runs on one replica at a time. processDue (ingest) still runs on every pod after the lock is released. Errors are still logged with the same messages, and the ISO collector keeps key 0xBEEF10A. processGmeetAutoImport is now also exported from ticks.js, but only for the test. Users will notice only one thing: Meet discovery and the ISO evidence sweep no longer cancel each other's ticks. The new test models Postgres session advisory locks across connections with a shared fake pool. It shows each job running while the other holds its lock, and that each job still runs on one replica at a time.
open_questions:
1. The finding also asks for a test that checks every numeric lock key is unique. That isn't done. Many jobs keep their LOCK_KEY private (learningNudge, monitoringRetention, usageOpenObservePush, opsMetricsPush, platformRetention, projectTaskDueNotifier, compliance/scheduler, and the other keys in ticks.js). So the test would either have to scan source text, which raises the lint:source-text ratchet, or export a key from each of those files, which is outside this lane. A follow-up could add a central registry module that all of these import, or move the remaining jobs to withNamedLock.
2. A hashtext(name) key and a numbered key share Postgres's int8 key space, so a clash is possible but very unlikely. That is the trade-off jobs/lib/namedLock.js already makes for its other users.

behaviour_notes: runComponent now kills a component child with SIGKILL after 10 minutes. It also kills it when stdout goes over 32 MB. In both cases the run rejects ("Component timed out after N ms" or "Component output exceeded N bytes"). executeWorkflow passes that error up the same way it passed an exit-code error before. stderr is now capped at 64 KB, and only in the "Component exited with code X: <stderr>" message; the run is not failed for it. Spawn errors on 'error' now reject the run, where before the promise could hang. An EPIPE on stdin is now ignored, so a child that exits early is reported through its exit code. stdout is decoded once over the whole concatenated buffer, which fixes multi-byte characters split across chunks. The limits are an optional third parameter (runComponent(path, inputs, {timeoutMs, maxStdoutBytes, maxStderrBytes})) that only tests use; every production caller keeps the defaults. The bundled components run in milliseconds to seconds, far inside both caps, so users notice nothing except that a hanging or flooding component now fails instead of hanging the request or chat turn.
open_questions: The 10-minute limit and the 32 MB cap are hard-coded constants. Should a self-hoster be able to change them with an env var? The kill reaches only the direct node child: grandchildren that a component starts itself are not in a killed process group. Spawning with detached and killing the group would close that, but it changes how the child is spawned, so I left it out.

tests_run: node --test on: auth/connectorSig.test.js (new, 8 pass), routes/webhooks/ncEvents.validation.test.js (15 pass; the 3 new replay/lookup tests fail against the HEAD version of ncEvents.js), routes/webhooks/ncEvents.rateLimit.test.js (new, 1 pass), routes/automation/events.{nextcloudTables,reactionRouting,spreadsheetFiles,webhookPayload}.test.js (all pass), routes/nextcloudStudioApps.test.js, routes/nextcloudTaskProcessing.validation.test.js, auth/connectorBootstrap.test.js (all pass), auth/accessRegistry.drift.test.js (21 pass; needs MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEY in env, so I ran it with a random throwaway value) and auth/accessRegistry.sweep.test.js (23 pass). npx eslint on all 6 changed files: clean. npm run typecheck (server): no errors.
behaviour_notes:
Only the connector-to-server calls change. Users and the UI see nothing new.

1. POST /auth/webhook/nc-user-sync now rejects a replay. If a valid signed request is sent again while its timestamp is still in the 5-minute window, the server answers 401 {"error":"Invalid or missing signature"} and the sync does not run. This is the same answer as any bad signature. A copy of the signature with the hex in upper case also counts as a replay.

2. The same route now has a per-IP rate limit. It uses the existing knob AUTOMATION_EVENTS_RPM_PER_IP (default 600 per minute), the same as /api/automation/events/*, and runs before the body is parsed. Over the limit the answer is 429.

3. On that route, a failing org lookup used to give a 500. It now gives the same 401 as an unknown org. /events/nextcloud already worked this way.

4. /api/automation/events/nextcloud keeps exactly the behaviour it had. Its private copy of the check is removed and it calls auth/connectorSig.verifyConnectorSig instead.

5. Replay protection is opt-in (`{ rejectReplay: true }`). Only nc-user-sync turns it on, so the task-processing and studio-apps callers behave as before. The signature check now exists in one place instead of three.
open_questions:
1. If Nextcloud fires the exact same event twice in the same second (for example two user.updated events for one ncUid from one profile save), both requests carry the same signature. The second one now gets a 401, which the connector writes to its log as a warning, and its sync is skipped. The first sync re-reads the user from Nextcloud and ncSyncBackstop reconciles later, so the effect should be nothing worse than log noise. If that warning is unwanted, the connector could add a per-request nonce to the signed body, but that is a change outside this lane.

2. The replay memory is per process, like the in-memory rate limiter. With several server replicas, a replay that reaches another replica is not caught. Closing that needs Redis: SET NX with a TTL.

3. /api/automation/events/nextcloud can still be replayed inside the 5-minute window, so it could fire automations twice. I did not turn on rejectReplay there. Identical file, Talk or table events in one second are plausible, and refusing them could drop automation runs, which is a behaviour change. A decision is needed on whether to opt it in, ideally together with a connector-side nonce.

4. The new nc-user-sync limit is the same 600 per minute per IP as the events limiter. A bulk import in Nextcloud (an LDAP first sync or a mass user import) could go over that. Events refused with a 429 are caught later by jobs/ncSyncBackstop.js. Raise the knob if that delay matters.

behaviour_notes:
userHasAnyWebpageAccess no longer reads an unordered `LIMIT 50` window and filters it in JS. It now runs one `SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1` EXISTS that applies the group-share rule in SQL, over every published page of the org.

What users notice: in an org with more than 50 published pages, a user whose only accessible page fell outside that window now gets the webpage tools in integrationTools and in the support-inbox available-integrations list. Before, they lost them (false negative only). Nothing that was granted before is denied now.

The group rule is the same as before. shared_groups is a TEXT column. A value that is NULL, `[]`, a JSON non-array, or not valid JSON counts as an entire-org publish, as parseJSON did. Otherwise one of the caller's groups must be on the page.

The CASE casts to jsonb only when the value starts with `[`. If that cast still throws (an array-looking value that is not valid JSON, which no writer produces), a log.warn fires and the old JS reading runs over `SELECT DISTINCT shared_groups`, so the answer stays the same.

The SQL works on PG15 (the deployed pgvector:pg15); it does not use pg_input_is_valid. No API shapes, status codes or UI changed.
open_questions: I did not do the second half of the fix in the record: removing userHasAnyStudioAppAccess (server/stores/studioAppStore.js:1066). It is outside this lane. It is also not fully dead: it is exported (studioAppStore.js:1568) and covered by studioAppStore.test.js:402-433, though no production caller uses it. It has the same unordered `LIMIT 50` + JS-filter bug. Whoever owns studioAppStore.js should either remove the function and its test assertions, or switch it to the same EXISTS. On studio_apps, shared_groups is already JSONB, so the predicate there is simpler: `jsonb_array_length(shared_groups) = 0 OR shared_groups ?| $2::text[]`. A small point: the SQL `?|` only matches string group ids. The publish route validates sharedGroups as an id list of strings, so this matches all data that can be written.

behaviour_notes: Gmail label.added automations now fire for every labelled message. Before the fix, one poll read only the first history page and at most 20 messages, then moved the cursor to the newest historyId, so the rest were silently dropped. Now the poller reads every page. It still handles at most 20 messages per tick, but when it hits that limit the cursor stops at the last history record it handled, so the next tick picks up the rest. Every message collected is dispatched, so a single tick can go slightly over 20 when the record that reaches the limit holds several messages. Multiple labels on one message are still grouped into one event. There is also a new warning log line when a tick hits the limit. mail.new works exactly as before: the paginated walk was moved unchanged into the shared helper automation/triggerBus/pollers/gmailHistory.js (walkGmailHistory), and both pollers now use it. No API, status code or UI changes.

tests_run: node --test stores/user/ncBindings.verification.test.js (new, 6/6; all 6 fail against the HEAD version of ncBindings.js); node --test auth/connectorBootstrap.orgHealth.test.js (17/17, 5 new route tests); node --test auth/connectorBootstrap.test.js (13/13); node --test auth/connectorBootstrap.ncuid.test.js (4/4); node --test stores/user/users.stageGuard.test.js (6/6, real schema incl. new DDL); npx eslint on all 5 changed files (clean); node scripts/typecheck.mjs (798 files, no errors)
behaviour_notes:
Every new code (resend, retarget, re-bootstrap) still resets the 5 guesses allowed per code. In addition, each pending verification row now has two lifetime budgets, counted per pendingId and not per IP:
- At most 5 codes may be sent (resend and retarget together).
- At most 30 guesses in total (5 x 6).

What a client could notice:
- **Resend or retarget after 5 sends, or after 30 guesses:** answers 429 `{ error, code: 'too_many_code_requests', remediation }` and sends no email. Before, this answered 200. The connector already passes a 429 with its code through to the user.
- **Verify after 30 guesses:** answers the existing 429 `too_many_attempts`, even for the right code. `attemptsLeft` is now the lower of the per-code and lifetime remainders; before 30 guesses this equals the old per-code value.
- **Re-bootstrap on a still-live row with a used-up budget:** no longer issues a new code or extends the expiry, so the row expires within 15 minutes. After that, a new bootstrap starts the row over with counters at 0.

Unchanged:
- The normal path (request a code, mistype, resend a few times, verify) works as before.
- A row that is not a pending verification still gets 410 `expired`.
- Successful responses keep the same shape.

Internal changes:
- `resetNcVerificationCode` and `retargetNcVerification` now return `{status:'ok',row}`, `{status:'not_eligible'}` or `{status:'too_many'}` instead of the row or null. Their only caller is `connectorBootstrap.js`.
- The caps are checked and incremented inside the UPDATE itself, so concurrent requests cannot overshoot them.

Schema: `schema.js` (outside my lane, a minimal edit) adds `verification_attempts_total` and `verification_code_sends` (`INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`) to `pending_nc_bindings` via an idempotent `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`.
open_questions:
1. **Rows can still be cycled by an attacker.** An attacker who controls a fake Nextcloud can claim up to `MAX_VERIFICATIONS_PER_ORG` (5) distinct nc_instance_ids per org. Each of those rows gets 30 guesses, and a fresh row only comes after the old one expires (15 minutes). That leaves roughly 600 guesses per 15 minutes per org. Before the fix this was unbounded; now it is bounded by time. Closing it would need an org-level failed-attempt budget, for example the sum of `verification_attempts_total` over the org's rows from the last 24 hours. I left that out because it lets an attacker lock a real org out of linking its Nextcloud, which is a behaviour trade-off for the owner to decide.
2. **Per-IP limiter left as is.** The XFF spoofing and `trustProxy: false` points in the evidence are not touched. The new caps no longer depend on the IP.
3. **Cap values.** I set 5 sends and 30 lifetime guesses per row. A legitimate admin who needs more than 5 code emails within one row's life now has to wait for the row to expire (at most 15 minutes after the last send) and retry from the connector.

behaviour_notes: I removed the local isPrivateAddress table. assertUrlIsPublic now judges each literal and each resolved address with the canonical core/http/ssrfGuard.isForbiddenAddress. The function's error texts, its return value (the parsed URL) and its call signature are unchanged. I added an optional second argument { lookup } so tests can inject DNS answers; no production caller passes it. The one visible change: a hostname whose DNS answer is an IPv4-compatible IPv6 address (::a.b.c.d), a hex-form IPv4-mapped address (::ffff:7f00:1) or 255.255.255.255 is now refused at the pre-check with the existing 'resolves to a private/loopback address' message. behaviour_notes: Only the operator CLI script server/scripts/cleanupAzureDuplicates.js changes; there is no change to the app, API or UI. The script used to check 4 hard-coded tables before deleting an orphan and counted any failed query as 0. It now builds the table list from the catalog once per run. It takes every base table in current_schema() that has an owner-style column (user_id, userId, owner_id, ownerId, owner_user_id, ownerUserId, created_by, createdBy, author_user_id, uploaded_by), plus every column with a foreign key to users(id). It refuses to delete an orphan unless the user has zero rows in all of those tables and every count succeeded. Without --force, any table whose count fails now blocks the delete. If the catalog query fails, or finds no tables at all, the script aborts before it changes anything. What an operator will notice: --apply without --force will skip some orphans it used to delete (for example ones that own notebooks, agents, PII-vault rows or connections). The output names each table, both those with data and those that could not be checked. There is also a new line "Checking orphans against N table(s)...". The --force behaviour is unchanged: it still deletes. The old 4-table check would have counted 0 for the test case where an orphan's only data is in notebooks, agents, PII vault and connections; the new test shows those rows are found and the delete is refused.
open_questions: 1) I did not change server/scripts/detachMisassignedFreeEmailUsers.js, which the record suggests should reuse the helper. It is outside this lane, and it only warns and never deletes users. It still has the same 4-table list and also counts errors as 0. Switching it to discoverUserTables/userDataFootprint is a small follow-up. 2) Audit-style columns (actor_id, updated_by, invited_by) are left out of the owner-column list on purpose. They are still counted when they have a foreign key to users(id). Any user_id column in audit or session tables now counts as data, so a typical SSO orphan with only login or audit rows will need --force where it did not before. If the owner wants such tables ignored, they could add an explicit ignore list to the helper. 3) Each orphan gets one full COUNT per discovered table. behaviour_notes: Both components now refuse private or internal targets. A URL whose host is loopback, RFC1918, link-local or metadata (localhost, metadata.google.internal, any numeric spelling), or a DNS name that resolves to such an address, now fails. The error is 'Refused: target resolves to a private/internal address.' (code EPRIVATEADDRESS). For the sitemap fetcher it is wrapped as 'Failed to fetch <url>: ...', or the sitemap is skipped as before. This also applies to every redirect hop and to sitemap or robots.txt URLs the site itself names. Schemes other than http and https fail with 'Unsupported protocol x:'. Public URLs behave as before: up to 5 redirects, 'Maximum number of redirects exceeded' beyond that, 'Request failed with status code N' for non-2xx (the sitemap fetcher still accepts 2xx and 3xx), and resolvedUrl is the final URL after redirects. Proxy support is kept. When HTTP(S)_PROXY or ALL_PROXY is set, the proxy dials, so each hop's name is resolved locally first and refused if it resolves to a private address; a name the local resolver cannot resolve is left to the proxy. website-sitemap-fetcher/index.js now runs main() only when started directly (require.main === module) and exports fetchUrl, parseSitemap and processSitemap. That changes nothing for the spawned CLI. Design: ssrfGuard.js in each component is a byte copy of server/core/http/ssrfGuard.js (it loads without undici). safeGet.js is byte-identical in both components. scripts/check-duplicated-files.mjs enforces all three pairs, and .jscpd.json ignores the copies (same precedent as agent-hub/src/shared/expr).
open_questions: 1) Proxy mode has no protection against DNS rebinding: the proxy resolves the name again, and a name only the proxy can resolve (intranet names in NO_PROXY or proxy DNS) is not checked. Closing that would require refusing names that do not resolve locally, which could break self-hosts whose only DNS is the proxy. 2) In proxy mode, a host matched by NO_PROXY is dialled directly by axios without the guarded lookup; only the local pre-flight check and the literal screen apply. 3) Nothing runs the component tests: ci.yml filters components/** into the server job, but run-tests.mjs only collects server/*.test.js. Wiring them in would need a change to ci.yml or run-tests.mjs (outside this lane). 4) Phase 4 of the plan should replace the hand copies with gen-shared-mirror. 5) Both component directories still carry undici transitively via cheerio. It is not used here (createGuardedDispatcher is never called).
